paras: The lynching of Bert Wilkinson took place at Silverton, Colorado, on the night of Sunday, September 4, 1881, when a party of masked men broke into the town jail, took out Wilkinson, who was accused of killing the city marshal, and hanged him. Wilkinson had been captured by Ike Stockton, a man described as his friend, and turned over to the San Juan County sheriff the day before. Papers across the country reported it as an outlaw's end, dwelling on his composure and on Stockton's betrayal.

In late August 1881, Silverton's city marshal, D. C. Ogsbury, was shot while trying to arrest Wilkinson and two companions, Dyson Eskridge and a Black man the papers called Jim Catrin, a "coon," "a negro boy," or the "Black Kid." The Tribune's Rico correspondent wrote that the three had come to Silverton after a saloon fight near Durango and that the dying Ogsbury named Wilkinson as his killer. Reports put the shooting between August 23 and 27. A Silverton dispatch said the whole town was aroused and that the men "will be lynched if captured."

The Black companion was taken first: according to a Denver wire, he surrendered and the Silverton Vigilance Committee hanged him the night after the murder, while the Tribune correspondent wrote that he was caught the next day, jailed, and taken out and lynched that evening. Rewards totaling $5,500 were offered for Wilkinson and Eskridge.

Wilkinson was captured on August 31 near Animas City. A Durango dispatch credited Marshal McCook and Deputy Sheriff Ike Stockton with the arrest and said Wilkinson was held under a guard of thirty men and then moved into the mountains "for fear of lynching by a party from" Durango or Silverton. The dispatch quoted him as wanting only a fair trial and added, "He is not likely to get it." His sister, Mrs. Flora W. Pyle, told the Dolores News that Stockton had posed as a friend helping the fugitives escape and then took Wilkinson at gunpoint for the reward.

On Saturday, September 3, the San Juan County sheriff took Wilkinson to Silverton and lodged him in jail. His sister stayed in town until Sunday and was told he would be hanged whether she stayed or not. Between 9 and 10 o'clock Sunday evening a party of masked men broke into the jail and took him out. By the correspondent's account he put the noose around his own neck, saying "Boys, I'll help you all I can," and kicked away the chair he stood on.

No report of an inquest or of arrests of the lynchers appears in the coverage. Stockton was shot by the La Plata County sheriff in Durango in late September and died, and Eskridge was captured in New Mexico; the Tribune correspondent expected Eskridge to meet "the fate of the 'Black Kid' and Wilkinson." A letter from Durango signed "Twenty-two of us" warned Silverton's mayor that the town's vigilantes had hanged the Kid, "who was innocent of any crime," and threatened vengeance if Eskridge were lynched.

Coverage came entirely from white papers. Colorado and New Mexico papers followed the manhunt, and the Fremont County Record closed the story in a line: the "Black Kid" and Wilkinson "are dead. Lynched." The Chicago Tribune's "Lynched" letter, reprinted in the Canton Advocate in Dakota, was the fullest account; it treated the hanging as "the closing scene of a most thrilling tragedy" in which Wilkinson "paid in full" for his crime.

The Richmond Dispatch headlined the story "A Blue-Blooded Outlaw," noting his Indiana family connections and calling the murder "wanton, brutal, and cowardly," while the Crawford Avalanche said he had killed "no less than three men." The Durango Southwest, quoted in the Las Vegas Gazette, said it did not approve of lynching but that dishonest officials made "strangling a necessity at times." Only the companion was marked by race in these stories; Wilkinson's own race was never stated.

Accounts of the capture differ: the Las Vegas Gazette first reported Stockton taking Wilkinson in the Needle mountains, a Durango dispatch put it on a mesa near Animas City, and a Denver wire said Eskridge was taken as well, which later reports contradicted.

bases: A party of masked men broke into the Silverton jail and hanged Wilkinson, held there by the San Juan County sheriff on a murder accusation (A16, A23, A24).

Masked men took Wilkinson from the sheriff's jail and hanged him for the killing of the town marshal, an act the papers called lynching (A16, A17, A23); the party's size is not given, but it is described as 'a party of masked men' and 'lynchers' (A16, A23).

The Chicago Tribune's Rico correspondent and the Colorado Fremont County Record independently report the lynching, and the Crawford Avalanche, Richmond Dispatch and a later Tribune letter agree (A16, A17, A18, A23, A24).

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'Lynched' letter called the hanging 'the closing scene of a most thrilling tragedy,' praised his 'utmost fortitude' and said he 'paid in full the debt' of his crime, while blaming Stockton's treachery.
The Richmond Dispatch's 'A Blue-Blooded Outlaw' called his crime 'wanton, brutal, and cowardly' and dwelt on his Indiana family and his bravado on the rope.
Colorado and Michigan briefs reported the lynching in a line ('are dead. Lynched.'; 'killed no less than three men').
The Durango Southwest, reprinted in Las Vegas, said it did not approve of lynching but that the lack of honest officials 'makes strangling a necessity at times.'
